examDifficulty.heading: Is the Tableau Data Analyst Exam Hard?
examDifficulty.summary: The Tableau Data Analyst exam is moderately difficult. It tests practical Tableau Desktop skills — not just feature awareness — so you need hands-on experience building visualizations, writing calculations, and configuring dashboard interactivity.
bullets: 45 questions in 90 minutes — roughly two minutes per question, which is comfortable for most candidates.
~70% passing score — you need approximately 32 correct answers out of 45 to pass.
LOD expressions are heavily tested — FIXED, INCLUDE, and EXCLUDE calculations require practice beyond reading documentation.
Hands-on Tableau Desktop experience helps most — candidates who have built real workbooks with calculated fields and dashboard actions pass at higher rates.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Book when you can confidently build LOD expressions, table calculations, and multi-sheet dashboards with filter actions without referencing documentation.

examFormat.heading: Tableau Data Analyst Exam Format Explained
examFormat.intro: The exam is proctored online or in-person. Here is the format:
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Scenario questions present a business question and ask you to choose the correct chart type, calculation method, or filter configuration to answer it.
bestWayToPass: Practice LOD expressions: Build FIXED, INCLUDE, and EXCLUDE calculations in Tableau Desktop until they feel intuitive — this topic appears frequently.
Memorize filter order: Know the filter order of operations (Extract, Data Source, Context, Dimension, Measure, Table Calculation) and when context filters change the outcome.
Chart selection logic: Know when to use bar, line, scatter, heat map, treemap, and dual-axis charts for different analytical questions.
Build interactive dashboards: Practice configuring Filter Actions, Highlight Actions, and URL Actions in multi-sheet dashboards.

certificationCard.description: Tableau Data Analysts analyze data and build actionable insights using Tableau. They connect to data, create calculations, and design visualizations that drive business decisions.

keyConcepts.h2: Tableau Data Analyst: Key Concepts for the Exam

blocks.heading: LOD Expressions (Level of Detail)
blocks.body: **LOD expressions** compute aggregates at a different granularity than the current view. FIXED computes at the specified dimension, ignoring view-level dimensions. INCLUDE adds dimensions to the view level (finer detail). EXCLUDE removes dimensions (coarser). LOD questions appear frequently — understand which to use for per-customer averages, cohort analysis, and ratio calculations.

blocks.heading: Context Filters
blocks.body: By default, Tableau applies filters in this order: extract, data source, context, dimension, measure. Adding a filter to context makes it run first, creating a temporary sub-table. Use context filters when you need a Top N filter to count only within a filtered subset — without context, Top N runs on the full dataset before other filters apply.

blocks.heading: Parameters and Dynamic Analysis
blocks.body: Parameters are workbook variables that users control via an input widget (slider, dropdown, etc.). They do not filter data by themselves — pair them with **calculated fields** to create dynamic filters, custom bins, or switchable measures. Parameter Actions (Tableau 2019.2+) allow clicking a mark to set a parameter value.

blocks.heading: Table Calculations vs LOD Expressions
blocks.body: **table calculations** (RUNNING_SUM, WINDOW_AVG, RANK, LAST) operate on the data already returned to the view — they cannot change which rows are in the view. **LOD expressions** run at query time and can affect which rows return. Use table calculations for running totals, percent of total, and period-over-period; use LOD for controlling granularity independently of the view.

blocks.heading: Live vs Extract Performance
blocks.body: Choose Live when data must be current to the minute (financial dashboards, operations). Choose Extract (.hyper) when query performance is critical and a scheduled refresh cadence is acceptable. **extracts** can be filtered at creation time to reduce size. Embedded credentials are required for scheduled extract refreshes on **Tableau Server** or Cloud.

scenarioTips.h2: How to Pass the Tableau Data Analyst Exam
scenarioTips.intro: The Tableau Data Analyst exam tests hands-on skills in building visualizations and analyzing data in Tableau Desktop. Focus on calculated fields, LOD expressions, chart selection, and dashboard interactivity.

blocks.heading: Chart Selection Logic
blocks.body: Know which chart type communicates each data story: bar (comparison), line (trend), scatter (correlation), heat map (density/pattern), map (geographic), and when to use combined or dual-axis charts.

blocks.heading: Calculated Fields & LOD Expressions
blocks.body: Know how to write basic **calculated fields** and the three LOD expression types: FIXED (independent of view), INCLUDE (adds granularity), and EXCLUDE (removes granularity). **LOD expressions** are heavily tested.

blocks.heading: Filters & Filter Order
blocks.body: Understand the filter order of operations: Extract → Data Source → Context → Dimension → Measure → Table Calculation. Know how context filters change which data other filters act on.

blocks.heading: Dashboard Interactivity
blocks.body: Know how to configure actions: Filter Actions (clicking to filter), Highlight Actions, and URL Actions. Understand how to design dashboards for mobile using device-specific layouts.

blocks.heading: Data Preparation in Tableau Prep
blocks.body: Know basic **Tableau Prep** operations: cleaning steps (data type changes, null handling, rename), aggregation steps, join/union steps, and how to output flows to **extracts** or published data sources.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the primary focus of a Salesforce Certified Tableau Data Analyst?
options: Only creating charts
Analyzing data and building actionable insights using Tableau
Managing Salesforce CRM
Marketing campaigns
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tableau Data Analysts analyze data and build actionable insights using Tableau for visualization and exploration.
whyWrong: 'Only creating charts' undersells the role, which spans full data analysis and insight-building, not just chart creation.
Managing Salesforce CRM is unrelated to the Tableau Data Analyst's analytics-focused role.
Marketing campaigns are unrelated to the Tableau Data Analyst's analytics-focused role.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Tableau capability is central to the Data Analyst role?
options: Only formatting
Data connection, preparation, calculation, and visualization for analysis
Server administration only
License management
sampleQuestions.explanation: Data Analysts use data connection, preparation, calculations, and visualization to deliver analysis.
whyWrong: 'Only formatting' undersells the role, which spans the full data workflow from connection to visualization.
Server administration alone is a narrower technical skill, not the core Data Analyst focus.
License management is an administrative task, unrelated to the Data Analyst's analytical role.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a FIXED LOD expression compute in Tableau?
options: A value filtered to the dimensions currently in the view
An aggregate at a specified dimension level, independent of the dimensions placed in the view
A running total across all rows in the dataset
A cross-database join between two sources
sampleQuestions.explanation: FIXED LOD expressions compute a value at the declared dimension granularity regardless of what dimensions are on the Rows/Columns shelves.
whyWrong: This describes a regular aggregate filtered by view dimensions — the opposite of FIXED, which ignores view dimensions.
A running total is a table calculation concept, not what FIXED LOD computes.
A cross-database join is a data-connection concept, unrelated to LOD expressions.

sampleQuestions.question: When should you add a Context Filter in Tableau?
options: To change chart colour formatting
When a Top N or condition filter needs to run on a pre-filtered data subset rather than the full dataset
To connect to a live database source
To create a dual-axis chart
sampleQuestions.explanation: Without a context filter, Tableau computes Top N across all data first, then applies other filters. Context filters reverse that order.
whyWrong: Context filters don't affect chart color formatting — that's unrelated to their function.
Context filters aren't about connecting to live data sources — that's a separate data connection setting.
Context filters aren't specifically for creating dual-axis charts — that's an unrelated visualization feature.

sampleQuestions.question: What is the main difference between a Live connection and an Extract in Tableau?
options: Live connections are less accurate than Extracts
Live connections query the data source in real time; Extracts are cached .hyper snapshots that are faster but need scheduled refresh
Extracts only work with Excel files
Live connections cannot be used on dashboards
sampleQuestions.explanation: Live connections deliver fresh data on every view load; Extracts trade real-time currency for faster query performance.
whyWrong: Accuracy isn't the differentiator — both connection types can be accurate; the difference is real-time versus cached/refreshed data.
Extracts work with many data source types, not just Excel files.
Live connections can absolutely be used on dashboards — this option denies a real capability.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a Tableau Parameter?
options: A filter that automatically removes rows from the view
A dynamic, user-controlled input value that can replace a constant in a calculation, filter, or reference line
A data source connection setting
A dashboard layout configuration option
sampleQuestions.explanation: Parameters accept user input at runtime — combine them with calculated fields or filters to create interactive, dynamic views.
whyWrong: A Parameter doesn't automatically remove rows — that's a filter's function, not a parameter's.
A Parameter isn't a data source connection setting — it's an input control used within calculations/filters.
A Parameter isn't a dashboard layout option — that's an unrelated dashboard configuration concept.

sampleQuestions.question: How is data blending different from a join in Tableau?
options: Blending is always faster than joining at the database level
Blending links two separate data sources at the view level on a common dimension; joining combines tables within the same data source at query time
Blending creates a permanent new combined data source
There is no practical difference between the two
sampleQuestions.explanation: Blending is useful when data lives in two different source systems and a database-level join is not possible — Tableau aggregates each source separately and combines results.
whyWrong: Blending isn't always faster than joining — performance depends on the specific scenario, not a fixed rule.
Blending doesn't create a new permanent combined data source — it links at the view level, not permanently.
There is a real, meaningful difference between blending and joining — this option denies it.

sampleQuestions.question: Which chart type best shows the distribution of a continuous measure across bins?
options: Pie chart
Histogram
Treemap
Gantt chart
sampleQuestions.explanation: A histogram groups continuous data into defined intervals (bins) and shows frequency — the standard chart for distribution analysis.
whyWrong: A pie chart shows part-to-whole composition, not distribution across bins.
A treemap shows hierarchical proportions, not the binned distribution a histogram specifically shows.
A Gantt chart shows timeline/duration data, not distribution of a continuous measure.

sampleQuestions.question: What does an INCLUDE LOD expression do that FIXED does not?
options: INCLUDE ignores all active filters in the view
INCLUDE adds specified dimensions to the view's level of detail before aggregating, computing at a finer granularity than the view alone
INCLUDE is only used with date dimensions
INCLUDE creates a table calculation on the result set
sampleQuestions.explanation: INCLUDE takes the view's dimensions and adds more — useful for computing per-member averages while the view aggregates at a higher level.
whyWrong: INCLUDE doesn't ignore filters — that's a mischaracterization of its actual behavior.
INCLUDE isn't limited to date dimensions — it works with any dimension type.
INCLUDE doesn't create a table calculation — it's a distinct LOD expression type.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a Filter Action in a Tableau dashboard?
options: A server-side filter applied automatically to all worksheets on load
An interactive action that passes selected marks as a filter to one or more target worksheets or dashboards
A data source filter that excludes null values globally
A context filter applied to a single worksheet
sampleQuestions.explanation: Filter actions allow users to click a mark and drill into filtered views — a core interactivity pattern in Tableau dashboards.
whyWrong: A server-side filter applied automatically to all worksheets describes a data source filter, not the interactive Filter Action being asked about.
A data source filter excluding nulls is a different, static filtering mechanism, not an interactive dashboard action.
A context filter applies within a single worksheet — it isn't the cross-worksheet interactive action being described.

sampleQuestions.question: How is a table calculation different from a regular aggregated measure in Tableau?
options: Table calculations run on the database before data is returned to Tableau
Table calculations run on the aggregated data already returned to the view, not on the underlying database rows
Table calculations are always computed faster than database aggregations
Table calculations cannot be used with date or time fields
sampleQuestions.explanation: Table calculations (RUNNING_SUM, WINDOW_AVG, RANK, etc.) operate on the result set in the view — not on source rows.
whyWrong: Table calculations don't run on the database — they run on data already returned to Tableau, the opposite of this claim.
Table calculations aren't inherently faster than database aggregations — that's not the defining characteristic.
Table calculations absolutely can be used with date/time fields — this option denies a real capability.

sampleQuestions.question: A user needs to compare year-over-year sales in a single view. Which Tableau approach is most appropriate?
options: Create separate worksheets for each year and place them side by side
Use a table calculation with percent difference from LOOKUP, or a FIXED LOD expression with a year dimension
Export the data to Excel and calculate manually
Add a separate context filter for each year
sampleQuestions.explanation: Percent difference table calculations or FIXED LOD expressions with year dimensions are the standard Tableau patterns for period-over-period comparison.
whyWrong: Creating separate worksheets per year doesn't allow direct comparison within a single unified view.
Manually exporting to Excel defeats the purpose of using Tableau's built-in calculation capabilities.
A separate context filter per year doesn't enable the year-over-year comparison calculation itself.

sampleQuestions.question: How do you create a dual-axis chart in Tableau?
options: Drag two dimensions onto the Rows shelf
Right-click the second measure pill on the Rows or Columns shelf and select Dual Axis, then synchronize axes if needed
Use the Marks card to manually overlay two chart types
Add a second data source as a blend and overlay the sheets
sampleQuestions.explanation: Dual Axis overlays two measures on independent axes in the same chart — right-click the second measure pill to enable it.
whyWrong: Dragging two dimensions onto Rows doesn't create a dual-axis chart — that's unrelated to the dual-axis mechanism.
Manually overlaying chart types via the Marks card isn't how dual-axis charts are actually created in Tableau.
Blending a second data source and overlaying sheets isn't the standard dual-axis creation method.

sampleQuestions.question: Which role in a Tableau deployment is responsible for certifying published data sources?
options: Tableau Desktop Specialist
Data Steward or content-certifying admin
Viewer licence user
Server hardware administrator
sampleQuestions.explanation: Certification is applied by Data Stewards or admins to published data sources, signalling to consumers that the data is authoritative and maintained.
whyWrong: Tableau Desktop Specialist is an entry-level certification, not a role responsible for certifying data sources.
A Viewer license user has read-only access — they don't have the ability to certify data sources.
Server hardware administration is an infrastructure role, unrelated to data source certification, which is a governance/content role.

sampleQuestions.question: What does a FIXED LOD expression compute?
options: Only table calculations
An aggregate at a specified dimension level, independent of the view
Only running totals
Only percentages
sampleQuestions.explanation: FIXED LOD computes at the dimension level you specify, ignoring filters and dimensions in the view (except context filters).
whyWrong: 'Only table calculations' misattributes FIXED LOD's function to a different Tableau feature.
'Only running totals' misattributes FIXED LOD's function to a different calculation type.
'Only percentages' misattributes FIXED LOD's function to a specific calculation type it isn't limited to.
